flow.say: Do your test. Then do the same for four more new tilts. Each time, say what your drawing predicts before you tilt.
flow.kid: Tilt the box as you planned. Write what happened. Do four more.

ask.q: Which tilt gave the biggest surprise, and what did it tell you?
good: The marble did not go where I said, so my drawing was wrong in some way.
The marble stopped in the middle, so there must be something there.
It rolled past where I thought the wall was, so there is a gap.

flow.parent: Expect the marble to roll freely along one side, stop with a click at a wall and pass through a gap at one end only. If the marble ever sticks in a corner, tilt the box the other way. If your child's drawing is already right, ask for a tilt that could show it wrong, for example along the very edge near the gap.

check.q: A tilt goes against your drawing. What is the best thing to do?
options: Tilt again until it fits the drawing
Change the drawing to fit the test
check.why: A model has to follow the evidence. Tilting until it fits the drawing, or blaming the box, protects the drawing instead of finding out the truth.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the changed model next to the first one, using a different colour for what changed. Ask for one more test of the new drawing with a new prediction. Write the result.
flow.say: Draw your model again, now that you have tested it. Show with a new colour what you changed. Then test the new drawing with one more tilt.
flow.kid: Draw your model again. Use a new colour for what you changed. Test it once more.

ask.q: What did you change in your model, and what test made you change it?
good: I added a gap, because the marble got through at one end.
I moved the wall, because the marble stopped sooner than I thought.
Any change tied to a particular test.

flow.parent: Praise the change, never the first drawing. Scientists change their models many times. A child who changes nothing can be asked to find a tilt that would test the weakest part of the drawing.

flow.do: Open the box and let your child compare the inside with both drawings. Ask what each drawing got right, what it left out, and what no tilt could have told you.
flow.say: Now open the lid. Look at your first drawing, your second drawing and the real inside. What did each one get right? What did every drawing leave out?
flow.kid: Open the box. Compare it with both drawings. What did you get right? What did you leave out?

ask.q: What could no tilt have told you about the inside of the box?
good: How high the wall is, because the marble stops the same for a low wall and a high wall.
What colour or what thing the wall is made of.
Anything the marble never touched, such as a corner.

flow.parent: Be honest if the child's model was different from the real box. A model that predicted every tilt correctly can still look different inside. The tilts could not tell the wall's height, colour or material. This is how it is for an atom, which nobody can open.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write the three parts: what I think, what I saw, why I think so.
flow.say: Finish with three short sentences. 'I think there is...' 'I felt and heard...' 'I think so because...'
flow.kid: Say or write what you think, what you felt and heard, and why.
flow.think: Scientists cannot open an atom the way you opened the box. How do they decide that their model of an atom is good?
flow.parent: Answers will vary. A strong answer ties the model to particular tilts, not just a feeling.

experiments.title: The blind-spot test: find the place in your eye that sees nothing
experiments.question: Can a dot in front of you vanish while your eye is open and the dot is still there?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. You will stare only at the cross while the paper moves closer. Will a dot 10 centimetres to the side stay in view? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: The same eye looks at the cross every time, and the other eye stays covered. The paper moves slowly towards the face and then away, always at the same pace. The test is done three times with each of two sheets, one blank and one ruled, because one try can be spoiled by a wandering eye. The head stays still and the eye stays on the cross.
results_table: Distance from my eye when the dot vanished (centimetres)
What I saw where the dot had been

materials.item: two sheets of paper, one blank and one ruled (a page from a notebook)
a thick black pen or marker
a ruler
a pencil for the results table

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw an eye from above with the nerve at the back and mark the blind spot. Write one sentence each for what you think, what you saw and why.
experiments.context: In this experiment you use a cross and a dot to find a small place in each of your eyes that sees nothing. You then find out what you see in its place, and ask whether what we see is a kind of model.

setup.art: A white sheet of paper with a small cross on the left and a black dot 10 centimetres to the right of it, with a ruler between them.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a cross and a dot, 10 centimetres apart. Make the dot about 1 centimetre across.

setup.art: A child holding the paper at arm's length with one eye covered by the left hand and the right eye looking at the cross.
setup.caption: 2. Cover your left eye. Look at the cross with your right eye. Do not look at the dot.

setup.art: A child's arm bending slowly to bring the paper closer, with a dotted line showing the distance and a ruler beside the child.
setup.caption: 3. Move the paper slowly closer. Stop when the dot vanishes.

setup.art: A ruled notebook page with the same cross and dot, and a hand covering one eye as the dot disappears and the lines run on.
setup.caption: 4. Repeat with the ruled sheet. Look at what fills the place where the dot was.

flow.do: Draw a cross on the left side of the blank sheet. Draw a black dot about 1 centimetre across, 10 centimetres to the right of the cross. Draw the same cross and dot, at the same distance apart, on the ruled sheet. Put the dot on a ruled line, so that a line runs through it.
flow.say: We will look for a place in your eye that cannot see. Do you think there is one? What would it feel like?
flow.kid: Draw a cross and a dot, 10 centimetres apart, on each sheet.
flow.parent: Make the dot a solid black circle, not a ring. Make the cross clear. The two marks must be 10 centimetres apart, measured from the middle of each.

flow.do: Ask for the prediction and the reason. Write it at the top of the page. Do not explain anything yet.
flow.say: Will the dot stay in view as I move the paper closer? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Will the dot stay in view? Why do you think so?
flow.parent: Most children say the dot will stay. That is the useful guess.

flow.do: Show your child how to do it. Cover the left eye with the left hand. Hold the blank sheet at arm's length with the cross straight in front of the right eye. Look only at the cross. Move the paper slowly towards the face, and then slowly away. Do this three times. When the dot vanishes, stop and measure the distance from the paper to the eye with the ruler. Write it in the table.
flow.say: Look at the cross only. Keep looking at it, even though you want to look at the dot. Move the paper slowly closer. Tell me when the dot goes.
flow.kid: Cover your left eye. Look at the cross. Move the paper slowly closer. Say stop when the dot goes.

ask.q: Where was the paper when the dot vanished? What did the place look like?
good: About arm's length less a hand, around 30 to 40 centimetres from my eye, and it looked like white paper.
The dot just went and the paper looked whole.
Any honest distance, and that the paper looked normal where the dot had been.

flow.parent: The dot usually vanishes at about 30 to 40 centimetres from the eye. If it does not vanish, keep the eye on the cross and move the paper more slowly. Check that the dot is on the same side as the open eye. If the left eye is covered, the dot is to the right of the cross. A very small child may need help to keep still. Expect most children to succeed in three or four tries. The distance is about 3.5 times the gap between the cross and the dot, so a longer gap makes the dot vanish farther away. Move the paper slowly and keep it from touching the face.

flow.do: Do the same with the ruled sheet, three times. Ask your child what is seen where the dot was.
flow.say: Now do the same with the ruled page. When the dot goes, look at where it was. What do you see there?
flow.kid: Try the ruled sheet three times. Look at where the dot was. What do you see?

ask.q: What did you see in the place where the dot had been on the ruled sheet?
good: The ruled line, running straight on, with no dot and no hole.
I saw the lines continue, as if nothing was missing.
Any honest answer that notes that no hole or black patch was seen.

flow.parent: The usual result is that the ruled line seems to run straight through the place where the dot was. The brain fills the gap with a guess made from the lines around it. Some children see a faint grey for a moment. That is fine.

check.q: On the ruled sheet, what did the dot's place look like?
options: A dark hole in the page
The ruled lines running straight on
check.why: People usually see the lines continue, not a hole. Choosing 'a dark hole' is the reading we expect before the test, so look again at what you actually saw.

flow.do: Switch to the other eye. Cover the right eye, look at the cross with the left eye and move the paper again. Ask your child where the dot has to be for this eye.
flow.say: Now try the other eye. Where do you think the dot should be this time, to the left or to the right of the cross?
flow.kid: Try the other eye. Put the dot on the other side of the cross.
flow.parent: For the left eye, the dot must be to the LEFT of the cross. Draw a new dot and cross for this, or turn the sheet over and draw them there. If your child enjoys this, let the child try it as an extra.

experiments.title: Torch and orange: use a model to explain day and night, then to predict the midnight Sun
experiments.question: Can a torch and an orange explain why day and night happen? Can they also tell us what happens in the far north, a place we have never seen?
experiments.predict: Before you tilt the orange, guess. If the orange leans towards the torch, will a dot right at the top ever go dark as the orange turns? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: The torch stays in one place, at the same height as the middle of the orange, about 50 centimetres away. The room is as dark as you can make it. The orange turns at the same slow pace each time, three full turns for each lean. Only one thing changes between tests: the lean of the pencil, which is straight up, leaning towards the torch, or leaning away from it.
results_table: What I predicted for the dot at the top
What happened to the dot at the top in three turns
What happened to the dot near the middle

materials.item: an orange, or any round fruit about 7 centimetres across
a sharpened pencil, a knitting needle or a thin bamboo skewer as the axle
a marker pen that writes on the skin of the orange
a phone torch or a small torch
a stack of books to hold the torch at the right height
a room that can be made dark, with the curtains drawn

experiments.record: Fill in the table for the three leans. Draw the orange, the torch and the pencil for each lean, and shade the lit half. Write one sentence each for what you think, what you saw and why.
experiments.context: Then you use it to predict what happens in the far north. This shows if the model can tell you what you did not already know.

setup.art: An orange with a pencil pushed straight through it from top to bottom, a small ring drawn round the top end and a dot drawn near the middle.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up pushes a pencil through the orange. Draw a small ring round the top for the far north, and a dot near the middle for your own place.

setup.art: A dark room with a phone torch on a pile of books and an orange on a pencil held 50 centimetres away, half lit and half in shadow.
setup.caption: 2. Darken the room. Hold the orange 50 centimetres from the torch. Half of it is lit.

setup.art: A hand turning the pencil so that the dot near the middle moves from the lit side into the dark side.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the orange slowly. Watch the dot go into the light and then into the dark.

setup.art: A hand holding the pencil leaning towards the torch at about 30 degrees, with the ring at the top fully lit while the orange turns.
setup.caption: 4. Now lean the pencil towards the torch and turn it again. Watch the ring at the top.

flow.do: Push the pencil through the middle of the orange from top to bottom. Draw a small ring about 1 centimetre across round the point where the pencil comes out at the top. Find the halfway point between the two ends of the pencil. Draw a dot on the side of the orange, about one finger-width above it. Put the torch on a pile of books. It must shine at the middle of the orange when the orange is held 50 centimetres away.
flow.say: This orange will stand for the Earth. The pencil is the line it spins on. The ring at the top is the far north. The dot is where we live. What will the torch stand for?
flow.kid: A grown-up pushes the pencil through the orange. Draw a ring at the top and a dot near the middle.
flow.parent: Use a sharp pencil and push gently, because a slippery orange can slide. The ring stands for the far north, and the dot for a place such as Kochi or Chennai, which are not far above the middle. Kochi and Chennai are only a little above the equator, so the dot should be near the middle.

flow.do: Turn off the room lights and close the curtains. Hold the orange by the pencil with the pencil straight up, 50 centimetres from the torch, and turn it slowly. Count three turns, and ask what happens to the dot near the middle. Write it in the table.
flow.say: Watch the dot as I turn the orange. When is it in the light? When is it in the dark? What does that make me think of?
flow.kid: Turn the orange slowly. Watch the dot. Say when it is in the light.

ask.q: Why does the dot go from light to dark and back again?
good: The orange turns, so the dot is carried into the light and then out of it.
The torch lights only one half, and the dot turns from one half to the other.
It is the same as day and night on the real Earth.

flow.parent: Half of the orange is lit and half is dark, with a soft edge between them. This edge is the dawn or the dusk. The dot goes from lit to dark once in each turn. Make sure the torch is at the same height as the middle of the orange, and keep the room dark. If your room cannot get dark, wait until evening and close the curtains.

check.q: Which turning of the orange makes your dot pass from day into night?
options: The torch moves round the orange
The orange turns while the torch stays still
The dot slides across the orange
check.why: In this model the orange turns and the torch stays still, like an Earth that spins. Moving the torch round a still orange gives the same lit half, but the real Sun does not circle us once a day.

flow.do: Ask for the prediction and the reason. Ask: if the pencil leans towards the torch, will the ring at the top ever go dark? Write what your child says before you try it.
flow.say: I will lean the pencil towards the torch. The ring at the top is the far north. As I turn, will it ever go dark? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Will the ring at the top go dark when the pencil leans? Say why.
flow.parent: Many children say yes, since everything went into the dark before. Do not say what will happen. The reason matters more than the guess.

flow.do: Lean the pencil towards the torch, about 30 degrees from straight up. That is about a third of the way towards the torch. Turn the orange slowly, three turns. Watch the ring at the top and the dot near the middle. Write what you see.
flow.say: Now the pencil leans towards the torch. Turn the orange. Watch the ring at the top. Does it go dark?
flow.kid: Lean the pencil towards the torch. Turn the orange. Watch the ring.

ask.q: Did the ring at the top ever go dark? What does that mean for a place in the far north?
good: No. It stayed in the light for all three turns, so a place in the far north would have daylight all day and all night.
The ring stayed lit while the dot near the middle still went into the dark.
Any honest answer tied to what was seen.

flow.parent: The ring stays in the light for every turn, while the dot near the middle still goes dark. This is the model's prediction: in the far north, in summer, the Sun does not set. This happens in northern Norway in June. The real Earth leans about 23.5 degrees. The orange leans more, about 30 degrees, to make the effect easy to see, and the ring is small to keep within the lit part. If the ring goes dark for part of a turn, lean the pencil a little more towards the torch or move the torch a little closer.

flow.do: Lean the pencil away from the torch by the same amount. Turn the orange three times. Watch the ring and the dot. Write what happens. Then set the pencil straight and look at the ring.
flow.say: Now lean the pencil away from the torch. What will the ring do? Try it and see.
flow.kid: Lean the pencil away from the torch. Turn the orange. Watch the ring.

ask.q: What happens to the ring when the pencil leans away from the torch?
good: It stays in the dark for all three turns.
The far north has night all day, which is a season of no Sun.
Any answer tied to what was seen.

flow.parent: With the lean away, the ring stays dark in every turn. In the real far north, this is the winter, when the Sun does not rise for weeks. With the pencil straight up, the ring sits on the line between the lit and the dark side, in a kind of twilight.

flow.do: Ask your child what the model got right, and what it left out or did wrong. Ask for one thing it cannot tell us.
flow.say: A model is never the whole truth. What did the orange and torch get right? What did they leave out?
flow.kid: Say what the model got right and what it left out.

ask.q: Name one thing the orange and torch leave out or get wrong.
good: The torch is much closer than the Sun, so its light spreads out, while the Sun's light is nearly parallel.
It has no seasons from going round the Sun yet, and no air or weather.
The orange leans more than the real Earth, which leans about 23.5 degrees.

flow.think: The model predicted the midnight Sun before anyone told you. Does that prove the model is how the Earth really works, or only that it is useful?
flow.parent: It predicted something true, but a model that predicts well is not proved to be right in every way. The real Sun is far away and its rays are nearly parallel. The real Earth also travels round the Sun. As an extra, walk the orange in a circle round the torch with the pencil always pointing at the same corner of the room. Watch the ring light up and go dark as you go round.

activities.title: Two maps of one home: different jobs, different models
activities.context: In this activity you draw the same home twice, for two different visitors. You find out that each drawing keeps what its reader needs and leaves out the rest.

materials.item: two sheets of paper
a pencil
coloured pencils or crayons

schedule.what: Draw a map for a delivery rider, draw a map for a friend who must find the water tap in the dark, and compare.

activities.record: Keep both maps. On the back of each, write one thing the map shows and one thing it leaves out.

setup.art: A child at a table drawing a simple map of a flat with a door, a corridor and a lift, with arrows.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the way from the building gate to your front door for a delivery rider.

setup.art: A second map of the same flat in the dark, showing a hand-wide path, the bathroom and a tap, with step counts.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the way from your bed to the water tap, for a friend who will walk it with the lights off.

setup.art: Two maps side by side, with a pencil pointing from one to the other.
setup.caption: 3. Put the maps side by side and say what each shows and what each leaves out.

flow.do: Give your child a sheet of paper. Ask for a map from the gate of the building to your front door. It is for a delivery rider who has never been here. If you live in a house, start from the street. Ask the child to put in only what the rider needs.
flow.say: Draw the way from the gate to our front door so that a stranger can follow it. Put in only what they need. What do they need?
flow.kid: Draw the way from the gate to your front door for a delivery rider.
flow.parent: Expect a line with turns, a lift or a staircase, floor numbers and the door. Leave out things like the plants, the colour of the walls and the furniture. Do not suggest what to draw.

flow.do: On a second sheet, ask your child to draw the way from the bed to the water tap. A friend will walk it with the lights off. Ask for things you can feel with the feet and hands, and for the number of steps.
flow.say: Now a friend must walk from the bed to the tap in the dark. What would they need to know that the rider did not? What do they not need any more?
flow.kid: Draw the way from your bed to the water tap. A friend will walk it in the dark.

ask.q: What did you put in this map that was not in the first one?
good: Steps counted, a doorway, and a bump or a rug that you can feel.
Things that feel different under the feet, not things that look different.
Any answer that shows the second map has a different reader.

flow.parent: Good answers count the steps, mark a door or a turn, a mat or a step down. A rider's map has no use for the mat. A walker in the dark has no use for the floor number.

flow.do: Put the maps side by side. Ask your child what each map shows, what each leaves out, and whether either is wrong.
flow.say: Which of these two maps is the right one? What does each leave out? Could one map do both jobs?
flow.kid: Put the maps side by side. Say what each shows and what each leaves out.

ask.q: Is either map wrong? Could one map do both jobs?
good: Neither is wrong, because each is right for its own reader.
One map for both jobs would be crowded and harder to read, so it would do each job worse.
Any answer that gives a reason.

flow.think: You drew your own home. What else about it did both maps leave out, and who would need that?
flow.parent: This is the idea of the lesson: every model leaves something out, and what it leaves out depends on its job.

activities.title: A photo and a diagram of a cut tomato
activities.context: In this activity you photograph a cut tomato and then draw a diagram of it. You compare them to find what a photograph keeps, what a diagram chooses, and what a diagram adds.

materials.item: a tomato, a bhindi (okra) or a lemon
a knife for a grown-up to use
a phone with a camera, or a drawing of what you see if there is no phone
paper and a pencil
a chopping board or a plate

schedule.what: Cut the fruit across, take a photo, draw a diagram with labels and arrows, and compare them.

activities.record: Keep the photo and the diagram. On the diagram, write one thing the photograph shows that the diagram does not, and one thing the diagram shows that the photograph does not.

setup.art: A tomato cut across on a plate, showing seeds in jelly in separate chambers.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts the tomato across, through the middle, and puts it on a plate.

setup.art: A phone held over the cut tomato, taking a photo from above.
setup.caption: 2. Take one photo from above. If you have no phone, draw exactly what you see, with every mark.

setup.art: A diagram of the cut tomato with plain lines, the labels 'skin', 'seed' and 'jelly' and an arrow.
setup.caption: 3. Draw a diagram of the tomato. Use plain lines, labels and one arrow.

flow.do: Cut the tomato across, through the middle, so that the seed chambers show. Put the halves, cut side up, on a plate in good light. Ask your child to look closely for one minute, then to say what is seen.
flow.say: Look closely at the cut tomato. What do you see? What do you wonder about?
flow.kid: Look closely at the cut tomato. Say what you see.
flow.parent: Use a knife yourself. The cut face shows a red skin, a thicker wall, and chambers with seeds in jelly. If you have no tomato, a lemon cut across shows segments and pips. A bhindi cut across shows a star-shaped ring of seeds.

flow.do: Take one photograph of the cut tomato from above. If there is no phone, ask your child to draw exactly what is seen, copying every mark, shine and seed.
flow.say: Take a photo that shows the cut tomato as it really is, with every mark on it.
flow.kid: Take a photo of the cut tomato from above.
flow.parent: The photo will show glints on the jelly, the juice, the shadow of the knife cut and one odd seed. That is the point.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw a diagram of the tomato on paper. It should have plain lines, a few clear labels, one arrow and no shading. Ask the child to choose which parts to keep.
flow.say: Now draw a diagram. Use plain lines. Give names to the parts. Add an arrow to show something. What will you keep, and what will you leave out?
flow.kid: Draw a diagram of the tomato with plain lines, labels and an arrow.

ask.q: What did you leave out of the diagram that is in the photograph?
good: The shine, the juice, the shadow and the odd marks.
The exact colour and the little bruise.
Anything that was in the photo but not needed for knowing the parts.

flow.parent: A good diagram has a clear outline, a few names such as skin, wall, seed and jelly, and an arrow. Leave out the shine and the juice. It might use a different colour for the seeds. If your child draws what they see, accept it and ask what they would leave out for a younger child.

flow.do: Lay the photo, the diagram and the real tomato side by side. Ask what the photograph is good for and what the diagram is good for. Then ask if the diagram could be used for a different tomato.
flow.say: Which one tells you what this one tomato looked like today? Which one helps you understand any tomato?
flow.kid: Compare the photo, the diagram and the tomato. Which is good for what?

ask.q: Which is better for knowing this tomato, and which for understanding all tomatoes?
good: The photo shows this one tomato as it looked today.
The diagram shows what every tomato of this kind has, with names for the parts.
Each is better for a different job.

flow.think: A diagram has labels and arrows that are not in the tomato. Are those parts of the model or parts of the tomato?
flow.parent: Make sure to eat the tomato afterwards, or put it in the compost.

activities.title: Walk the solar system: a model that is true to scale
activities.context: In this activity you lay out the Sun and the planets true to scale along a street, a park or a long corridor. You find out what every picture of the solar system must leave out.

materials.item: a football or a ball about 22 centimetres across, or a steel plate that size
two mustard seeds, two poppy seeds (khus khus) or pinheads, and a marble, to stand for five planets
chalk or small pieces of paper to mark each place
an open, safe path at least 100 big steps long, such as a park, a school ground or a long terrace
a pencil and paper

schedule.what: Place the Sun and the first four planets by pacing out the distances, then think about the rest.

activities.record: Write down the number of big steps for each planet. Beside it, write one thing that your usual diagram of the solar system left out.

setup.art: A child holding a football at the start of a long paved path, with a mustard seed on a small piece of paper beside the ball.
setup.caption: 1. Put the Sun, a football, at the start. Put the Earth, a mustard seed, 32 big steps away.

setup.art: A path with five marks in a line at different distances, labelled Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars and Jupiter.
setup.caption: 2. Mark the others with chalk. Mercury is 12 steps, Venus 23, Mars 48 and Jupiter 164.

setup.art: A child standing by the football and looking down the long path to a small speck far away.
setup.caption: 3. Look from the Sun. Can you even see the Earth?

flow.do: Take your things to a safe open path. Put the football on the ground as the Sun. Say that 1 step in the model stands for a big adult step of about 75 centimetres. Check the steps work by pacing out 10 steps and measuring them against 7 or 8 metres if you have a tape.
flow.say: Here is the Sun, the size of a football. We shall put the planets at their true distances. What size do you think the Earth should be? How far away?
flow.kid: Put the football down as the Sun. Guess how far away the Earth should be.

ask.q: Guess first. How many big steps from the football should the Earth be?
good: Any guess, then compare with 32 steps.
A guess that gives a reason, such as 'far, because the Sun is hot'.

flow.parent: The scale is simple. If the Sun is 22 centimetres across, the Earth is 2 millimetres across and 24 metres away. One big adult step is about 75 centimetres, so 24 metres is about 32 steps. The distances are these. Mercury is about 9 metres (12 steps), Venus 17 metres (23 steps), Earth 24 metres (32 steps) and Mars 36 metres (48 steps). Jupiter is 123 metres (164 steps). Saturn is 226 metres, Uranus 454 metres and Neptune 711 metres.

flow.do: Pace out the distances for Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars and Jupiter. Mark each place with chalk or a piece of paper. Put a poppy seed at Mercury and at Mars. Put a mustard seed at Venus and at the Earth. Put a marble at Jupiter.
flow.say: Walk 12 steps. Put down the smallest seed. That is Mercury. Now 23 steps from the Sun for Venus. Keep going.
flow.kid: Pace out the planets. Put a small thing at each place.

ask.q: What do you notice about how far apart the planets are, compared with how big they are?
good: They are far apart, and almost all of the space is empty.
The planets are tiny beside the Sun and the gaps are huge.
Any answer tied to the pacing.

flow.parent: The Earth is a seed 32 steps from a football. Jupiter, a marble that is a little too small for its true size of about 2 centimetres, is 164 steps away. If your path is too short for Jupiter, stop at Mars and say how much farther Jupiter would be. Do not run, and keep to the safe path.

flow.do: Stand at the Sun and look at the Earth's seed. Then ask your child to look at a diagram of the solar system in a book or on the phone. Ask what the diagram does to the distances and sizes, and how it could say so honestly.
flow.say: Look back at the Sun from the Earth. Then look at a picture of the solar system. What does the picture change so that it fits on a page?
flow.kid: Look back at the Sun from the Earth. Compare it with a diagram. What did the diagram change?

ask.q: What does a diagram of the solar system have to change to fit on a page, and what should it say?
good: It squashes the distances and makes the planets bigger, and it should say 'not to scale'.
It makes the planets much closer and bigger than they are.
Any answer that names the change and the words 'not to scale'.

flow.think: No page can show the solar system true to scale. Is a diagram that cheats still a good model?
flow.parent: Pick the seeds up afterwards, so that no small objects are left behind. If the Sun is a steel plate, wash it after use.

activities.title: The heart is like a pump: where does the likeness stop?
activities.context: In this activity you test the comparison 'the heart is like a pump'. You use a soap pump and your own pulse to find where the likeness holds and where it stops.

materials.item: a soap dispenser or a spray bottle with a pump
a steel bowl of water
a watch or phone with a clock showing seconds
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Pump the bottle and feel the pulse, count the beats before and after star jumps, and find where the comparison stops.

activities.record: Draw two columns headed 'Like a pump' and 'Not like a pump'. Write at least two things in each column.

setup.art: A child pumping a soap dispenser with water inside, over a steel bowl, while counting.
setup.caption: 1. Pump the bottle 10 times, with a pause between. Watch what comes out each time.

setup.art: A child's two fingers resting on the inside of the other wrist, with a clock in view.
setup.caption: 2. Find your pulse and count the beats in 15 seconds.

setup.art: A child doing star jumps on a mat, then counting the pulse again.
setup.caption: 3. Do 20 star jumps, count the pulse again, and compare.

flow.do: Fill the dispenser with plain water. Pump it 10 times into the steel bowl. Ask your child to watch the water and to say what a pump does. Ask where the water comes from, what makes it move and what makes it stop.
flow.say: Pump the bottle ten times. What does the pump do to the water? What do you have to do to make it work?
flow.kid: Pump the bottle ten times. Say what the pump does to the water.

ask.q: What does a pump do, and what does it need to keep working?
good: It pushes liquid along, and it needs a push each time, from a hand or from a motor.
It has a part that squeezes and lets go, again and again.
Any answer that names pushing liquid and needing something to push it.

flow.parent: Wash the bottle afterwards and do not drink the water. A tap with a soap pump gives the same picture.

flow.do: Ask your child to find the pulse on the inside of the wrist, below the thumb. Count the beats for 15 seconds, sitting still. Multiply by 4. Then do 20 star jumps, count again, and multiply by 4. Write both numbers.
flow.say: Find your pulse. Count the beats for 15 seconds. Then do 20 star jumps and count again. What changed?
flow.kid: Find your pulse. Count for 15 seconds. Do 20 star jumps. Count again.

ask.q: What happened to your pulse after the jumps, and what does the heart do about it?
good: It went faster, because the heart beats faster when the body needs more.
The heart pumps harder or faster when the muscles need more blood.
Any honest answer tied to the numbers.

flow.parent: A child's resting pulse is usually 70 to 100 beats a minute and goes up to 120 to 160 after exercise. A pump that speeds itself up and slows itself down when the body needs it is not like a hand pump. Press with two fingers and not the thumb, because the thumb has its own pulse. Stop the star jumps if your child feels dizzy or short of breath. A child with a heart or breathing problem should skip them and only count the resting pulse.

flow.do: Draw two columns. In the first, ask your child to list what is like a pump about the heart. In the second, what is not. Use the pump and the pulse.
flow.say: Where is the heart like a pump? Where is it not? Look at what you found.
flow.kid: Make two lists. Where is the heart like a pump? Where is it not?

ask.q: Where does the likeness stop?
good: A pump needs a hand or a motor, but the heart beats by itself.
A soap pump never speeds up by itself. The heart does.
The heart is a living part of a body, and grows and mends itself. A pump is made and does not.

flow.think: The pump helped us understand the heart, but the heart was there long before pumps. What does that tell us about the pump as a model?
flow.parent: Real likeness: the heart has valves that let blood flow one way, as a pump does. It squeezes and lets go. It pushes liquid through tubes. Real differences: it is alive, it beats without a hand, and it speeds up and slows down on its own.

activities.title: Peel an orange: why a flat map must stretch
activities.context: In this activity you draw on an orange and peel it. You will see why a flat map of the round Earth must stretch or tear some part.

materials.item: an orange or any round fruit with a loose skin
a marker pen
a plate
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Draw a small shape on the orange, peel it, press the peel flat and see what happens to the drawing.

activities.record: Draw what the shape looks like on the flat peel. Write one sentence about what happened to it.

setup.art: An orange with a marker-drawn outline of a rounded shape and a straight line across the middle.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a circle, a square and a long line across the orange.

setup.art: An orange peel pulled off in one piece and laid in a rough star shape on a plate.
setup.caption: 2. Peel the orange carefully, trying to keep the skin in one piece.

setup.art: A hand pressing the peel flat on the plate, with the skin tearing at the edges and the drawings stretched.
setup.caption: 3. Press the peel flat. Look at what happens to your shapes.

flow.do: Use a marker to draw a circle and a square, each about 3 centimetres across. Draw a long line from the top to the bottom of the orange. Ask your child what will happen to them when the skin is flattened.
flow.say: Draw a circle, a square and a line down the orange. What will happen to them if we press the peel flat?
flow.kid: Draw a circle, a square and a long line on the orange. Guess what will happen.
flow.parent: Draw with a light hand, because the skin can be oily. Use a dark marker. Ask for the guess and the reason before the peeling.

flow.do: Peel the orange by hand, using your thumb. Try to keep the skin in as large a piece as you can. Lay the pieces on the plate. Press them flat with the palm and look at the drawings.
flow.say: Peel the orange. Press the peel flat. What happens to the circle, the square and the line?
flow.kid: Peel the orange. Press the skin flat. Look at your drawings.

ask.q: What happened to your shapes when you flattened the skin?
good: The skin split or stretched, and the shapes were pulled out of shape.
The line broke into pieces, and the circle stretched at the edges.
Any answer that says what happened to the shapes.

flow.parent: Citrus peel always tears when pressed flat because it is a curved surface. A round ball cannot be flattened without stretching or tearing. This is true of the Earth. If your skin tears at once, that is a good result: you can say that is where a map must cut or stretch.

flow.do: Ask your child to look at a flat map of the world or a page in a school atlas. Ask where it stretches, and how the map-maker had to choose.
flow.say: A flat map of the world has the same problem as your peel. Where do you think it stretches? Look at Greenland and Africa.
flow.kid: Look at a flat world map. Where do you think it stretches?

ask.q: Why can no flat map of the Earth be right in every way?
good: A round surface cannot be flattened without stretching or tearing something.
Every map-maker has to choose which thing to keep true, such as shapes or areas.
Any answer tied to the orange peel.

flow.think: Every flat map must be wrong in some way. How would you choose which way it is wrong?
flow.parent: Greenland looks about as large as Africa on the map of most classrooms, but Africa is about 14 times larger. A globe has no such problem, but you cannot fold it into your pocket. Eat the orange afterwards.

projects.title: The map that a stranger can follow: draw, test, fix
projects.context: In this project you draw a map of a short route and give it to someone who has never walked it. You see where they go wrong and fix the map. You find out that a good model is made by testing it on other people.

materials.item: paper, a pencil and a rubber
coloured pencils
a short safe route, such as from your door to the building gate, a shop in the lane or a park gate
two people who do not know the route well, such as a relative, a friend or a neighbour, each at a different time
a phone with a map, for the last day

schedule.what: Walk the route with a grown-up, noticing what you pass. Then draw your first map from memory.
Give the map to the first helper, a person who does not know the way, and watch where they go wrong or ask questions. Do not help.
Fix the map using what you saw. Give the new map to a second helper.
Compare your final map with a phone map of the same route. List what each shows and leaves out.

projects.record: Keep every version of the map. Write down every place where the helper hesitated or went wrong. Write one sentence about what you changed and why.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up walking along a lane from a front door to a gate, with the child noting a tree and a tap.
setup.caption: 1. Day 1: walk the route once and notice what you pass.

setup.art: A child's first map with a wiggly line, a tree and a tap, in pencil on lined paper.
setup.caption: 2. Day 1: draw the first map from memory.

setup.art: A neighbour holding the map and looking up at a corner while the child watches and takes notes.
setup.caption: 3. Day 2: a helper tries the map while you watch and do not help.

setup.art: Two maps of the same route side by side, one in pencil and one on a phone screen.
setup.caption: 4. Day 4: compare your final map with the phone's map.

flow.do: Walk a short, safe route with your child to a place within sight, such as the building gate. Ask your child to notice what could help a stranger find the way. Back home, ask for a map of the route drawn from memory. It needs a start, an end and any signs along the way.
flow.say: Walk to the gate and notice what helps you know where you are. Then draw a map of the way, so that someone who has never been here could follow it.
flow.kid: Walk the route with a grown-up. Then draw a map of it from memory.

ask.q: What did you decide to put in your map, and what did you leave out?
good: The turns, a tree, a tap and a staircase, because a stranger could use these.
Not the colour of the walls or the people, because they change.
Any answer that gives a reason for each thing.

flow.parent: Choose a route that is safe and short, and stay beside your child. Do not tell your child what to put on the map, even if it is missing things. Day 2's test will show what is missing.
flow.wait: Leave it until the next day

flow.do: Give the map to a helper who does not know the route. Ask them to follow it, saying aloud what they see and where they are not sure. Walk behind them. Do not help or say anything. Write down every place they stop, go wrong or ask a question.
flow.say: Give this map to a friend who does not know the way. Watch. Do not help. Write down every place where they get stuck.
flow.kid: Give your map to a helper. Watch them follow it. Do not help.

ask.q: Where did the helper go wrong, and what in the map made it happen?
good: At a turn, because the map did not show which way to turn.
At a place where the map had no sign, so there was nothing to check against.
Any answer that links a mistake to something in the map.

flow.parent: Stay quiet, even if the helper is clearly lost. Their mistakes are the useful part. A route that is too long makes this hard, so end the test after five minutes. Stay with them the whole time.
flow.wait: Leave the fixing until the next day

flow.do: Ask your child to fix the map, using every note from the helper's test. Ask for a new copy with the changes in a different colour. Give the new map to a second helper and note again where they stop.
flow.say: Look at your notes. What will you add? What will you change? Draw the new map. Then try it on someone else.
flow.kid: Fix your map using your notes. Try it on a second helper.

ask.q: Did your fixed map work better? How can you tell?
good: The helper stopped fewer times or went straight to the place.
The helper used the new sign I added.
Any answer that points to something counted or seen.

flow.parent: Praise the fixing more than the first map. If the second helper still goes wrong, count that as useful data and ask what the map would need.

flow.do: Open a phone map of the same route. Lay your final map beside it. Ask your child to list what each one shows well and what each leaves out. Then ask which is better for a stranger on foot, for a driver and for someone in a wheelchair.
flow.say: Look at your map and the phone's map of the same route. What does each show? What does each leave out? Which is better for which person?
flow.kid: Compare your map with the phone's map. Say what each leaves out.

ask.q: Is your map or the phone map the better one?
good: Neither is better for everything. Mine has the tap and the tree. The phone's has the exact distances.
It depends on who is using it and for what job.
Any answer that gives a job and a reason.

flow.think: You made a model and then tested it on other people. Why do scientists also want other people to test their models?
flow.parent: The aim is that the child sees what a model for a particular person needs. The phone map may leave out steps, tap and trees, and show roads. Yours may leave out distances.

challenges.title: A touch map for someone who cannot see it
challenges.context: This is a design problem. Some people cannot see a drawing, so a map must be made that they can read by touch. You build a model of your home that a blind or low-sight person could follow with their fingers.
challenges.problem: Make a map of your home, from the front door to the kitchen, that a person who cannot see can read with their fingers. It must show the walls, the doors and the way. There is more than one good answer.
constraints: Use only things you can find at home, such as card, string, rice, sandpaper, tape, cloth and pulses.
Anything the map shows must feel different from the things around it.
Your map must fit on one sheet of card, which is about the size of a newspaper page.
A friend with their eyes shut must follow it, with a grown-up watching, and find the kitchen.
Include a key that tells by touch what each material means.
materials: a big sheet of card or the lid of a shoebox
string, wool or a strip of cloth
rice, dal or sand, glued in patches
glue, tape and scissors for a grown-up
a bandana or a clean scarf to cover the eyes of the tester

setup.art: A child at a table with a big card, string and pulses spread out, beside a plan of a small flat drawn in pencil.
setup.caption: 1. Plan your home on paper first, and choose which materials stand for which things.

setup.art: A card map with string walls, a patch of rice for the kitchen and a strip of sandpaper for the corridor.
setup.caption: 2. Build the map. Make walls, doors and rooms feel different.

setup.art: A girl with a scarf over her eyes tracing a string wall on the card map with two fingers while a parent watches.
setup.caption: 3. Test the map. A friend with their eyes shut follows it by touch.

flow.do: Say that some people read with their fingers. Ask your child what a map for them would need that a drawn map does not. Ask the child to sketch a plan of the route from the front door to the kitchen. Then ask which material will stand for a wall, a door, the route and the kitchen.
flow.say: Imagine a person who cannot see this map. What would they use instead of their eyes? What things must feel different from each other?
flow.kid: Plan the map. Pick a feel for walls, doors, the route and the kitchen.

ask.q: Which things on a map must feel different from each other, and why?
good: Walls, doors and the route, because a person has to tell them apart without seeing.
Rough for a rug or a step, smooth for a clear floor.
Anything that has a reason.

flow.parent: A touch map is a real tool. Many schools and railway stations in India have raised maps. The point is that a different reader needs a different model of the same place.

flow.do: Ask your child to build the map. Glue string for the walls, rice for the kitchen, sandpaper for a rough floor and a strip of cloth for the route. Keep walls and doors different. Add a key made of the same materials.
flow.say: Now make the map out of things you can feel. Walls are string, rooms are patches. Make a key out of the same things, so that the reader knows what each feel means.
flow.kid: Build the touch map. Make a key from the same materials.

ask.q: What did you use for the key, and how can a person know it is the key?
good: A small patch in one corner for each material, in the same order each time.
Each material is shown next to a bit of string.
Any key that can be found by touch alone.

flow.parent: Glue and scissors are for the grown-up. Let the glue dry for 10 minutes before the test. Rice is the cheapest way to make a patch. If you have no rice, use dal or sand.

flow.do: Cover a friend's or family member's eyes with a scarf. Ask them to follow the map with two fingers from the front door to the kitchen. Watch where they pause. Write down each pause.
flow.say: Put on the scarf and follow the map with your fingers. Tell us what you feel. Where does it get hard?
flow.kid: Cover your eyes. Follow the map by touch. Say where it gets hard.

ask.q: Where did your tester get stuck, and what would make the map better?
good: At a place where two materials felt too alike, so I would make them more different.
At a doorway that felt like a wall, so I would raise the walls.
Any answer that links a stuck place to a change.

flow.parent: Make sure that the tester sits safely and cannot fall. The test is meant to find mistakes. Ask the tester to say aloud what they feel.

flow.do: Ask your child to improve the map once, using what the tester found. Then ask what the map leaves out, and whether that matters for a person who cannot see.
flow.say: Fix one thing that did not work. What does your map still leave out? Does that matter for the person using it?
flow.kid: Fix one thing. Say what the map still leaves out.

ask.q: What does your map leave out that a blind person might need?
good: Furniture, steps or things in the way, which could be added as small bumps.
Sounds and smells, which many blind people use. A map could use a different smell for the kitchen.
Any answer that thinks about the reader.

flow.think: A map for fingers has a different job from a map for eyes. What else could a map use besides sight and touch?
flow.parent: Blind people read a place by touch, sound, smell, memory and a stick or a dog. A sighted person's map shows only one of the ways.

general: Glue string for the walls. Use a rough patch of sandpaper for the floor of the corridor, so that the walls and the route feel different.
Use a raised line for the way and a different patch for each room, with a key made of the same patches in a corner.
Mark the doors by leaving a gap in the string wall and putting a bead in the gap.
creative: Use a different smell for each room. Put a dab of cardamom on cotton for the kitchen and a dab of coconut oil on cloth for the bedroom. Then the reader's nose helps their fingers. Check first that nobody at home is allergic to the smells.
Make the map out of a cloth that folds, so that it can be carried. A corridor can then be pulled out and felt in its full length.
Add small bells or a rattle of dal in a sealed packet at the door, so that the reader can feel and hear where they are.
challenges.your_turn: Make your own touch map in a way that nobody here has thought of. What did you choose to leave out, and who decided it should be left out?

challenges.title: Test a model bridge before you build: the strongest paper bridge
challenges.context: This is a design problem. Engineers test small models before they build a real bridge, because a mistake in a real one costs lives. You make test models of a paper bridge, load them with coins and find the strongest shape.
challenges.problem: Build the strongest bridge from one sheet of ordinary paper across a gap of 15 centimetres. The strongest holds the most coins in a small cup. There is more than one good answer.
constraints: Use one sheet of A4 paper, or a page of the same size from a notebook, for each bridge. Tape may join the paper to itself, but must not stick the bridge to the books.
The bridge must rest on two piles of books with a gap of 15 centimetres between them, with 2 centimetres of paper on each side.
Load the bridge by adding coins one at a time to a light cup in the middle, and count how many it holds. Use one kind of coin, such as one-rupee coins, so that the counts can be compared.
Test each shape at least twice and write down both numbers.
Make at least three different shapes and predict how many coins each will hold before you test it.
materials: two piles of books of equal height
a light cup, such as a paper cup or a small plastic cup
about 40 coins of the same kind, for example one-rupee coins

setup.art: Two piles of books with a gap of 15 centimetres between them and one flat sheet of paper lying across the gap, with a cup on top.
setup.caption: 1. Set up two piles of books 15 centimetres apart, and lay a flat sheet across.

setup.art: Three paper bridges side by side: a folded zigzag, a rolled tube and an arch.
setup.caption: 2. Make three shapes of bridge from the same size of paper.

setup.art: A child adding a coin to the cup on a folded paper bridge, with a counting row of coins beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Add coins to the cup one at a time, counting, until the bridge bends or falls.

flow.do: Build the test stand. Put two piles of books, the same height, 15 centimetres apart. Lay one flat sheet across the gap with about 2 centimetres on each side. Put the cup in the middle and add coins one at a time. Count how many it holds before the paper sags or falls.
flow.say: First try a flat sheet. How many coins do you think it will hold? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Lay a flat sheet across the gap. Guess how many coins it will hold.

ask.q: Guess first. How many coins will the flat sheet hold?
good: Any guess with a reason, for example 'just one or two, because it is thin'.
A guess that compares with a folded one.

flow.parent: A flat A4 sheet will usually sag with the empty cup, or hold only a coin or two. This is the first model and the one to beat. Measure the books to make sure the gap is the same each time.

flow.do: Ask your child to make two more shapes from a sheet each. One may be an accordion fold, like a paper fan, with 8 to 10 pleats each about 1 centimetre deep. Another may be a roll into a tube. For each, ask for a prediction, then test it with coins and write the result.
flow.say: Make two new shapes. Before you test each one, say how many coins it will hold. Then test it.
flow.kid: Make two new bridges. Predict each one. Test with coins.

ask.q: Which shape was strongest, and was it the one you predicted?
good: The folded one held the most, because folds stiffen paper.
The tube held a lot, because a curved shape is hard to bend.
Any honest answer, whether or not it matched the guess.

flow.parent: A pleated bridge usually holds many times what a flat sheet does. How many coins depends on the paper and the coin, so compare your own shapes with each other and do not expect our numbers. A tube may be stronger or weaker, depending on how it is held in place, so ask your child to hold or tape the ends. Stop adding coins when the bridge sags a lot or falls. Do each test twice and use both numbers.

check.q: A bridge held 20 coins in one test and 12 in a second. What is the best thing to do?
options: Do it a third time and use the middle value
check.why: One test can be spoiled by a small difference in how the coins were added. A third test, and the middle value, tells you more than choosing the number you like best.

flow.do: Ask your child to improve the best bridge once. Ideas are a deeper fold, a tube inside a fold, or two layers of paper. Test it twice. Write what changed.
flow.say: Take your strongest bridge and make it stronger. What will you change? Predict, then test.
flow.kid: Improve your best bridge. Predict. Test it twice.

ask.q: What change made it stronger, and why do you think so?
good: Deeper folds, because a deep fold is harder to bend.
Two layers, because there is more paper to carry the load.
Any change with a reason.

flow.parent: A fold makes the paper deeper, and a deeper beam is much harder to bend, even when it is made of the same paper.

flow.do: Ask what the paper model cannot tell us about a real bridge made of steel. Ask what an engineer would still need to test.
flow.say: Your paper bridge held coins. Will a steel bridge behave the same way? What can your test not tell us?
flow.kid: Say what a paper test cannot tell you about a real bridge.

ask.q: What can a small paper model not tell us about a real bridge?
good: How steel bends, because paper and steel are different.
How wind and a moving crowd would shake it.
How big things change, because a bigger bridge carries more weight in itself.

flow.think: The real bridge costs a very great deal. What other things could we test in a model before building the real one?
flow.parent: Engineers use small models and computers before building. The model leaves out the material, the size, the wind and the crowd. That is why they use several tests.

general: Fold the paper into an accordion of 8 to 10 pleats, so that each fold is a small beam that resists bending.
Roll the paper into a tube and tape its edge, which is stiff because a curved shape is hard to bend.
Fold two edges up to make a channel, like a gutter, so that the paper has a deep edge on each side.
creative: Fold a zigzag and glue a flat strip, cut from the same sheet, over the top. This makes a hollow box of folds, like the hollow beams of real bridges.
Glue several thin paper tubes side by side, as bamboo tubes are tied together in a real footbridge.
Curve the paper into an arch with its ends against the books, so that the load pushes the ends outward. Put a heavy book against each end so that the ends cannot slide.
challenges.your_turn: Design a bridge of your own from one sheet of paper that nobody here has tried. Predict how many coins it will hold, and test it.

games.title: The right model for the job: a card game for 2 to 4 players
games.context: This is a card game about choosing a model. Every job card describes a job, and you pick the model card that suits it best. You score for a good choice and for an argument, and you learn that no model suits every job.

setup.art: A table with a pile of 16 job cards face down and ten model cards face up in a row.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the 16 job cards and the 10 model cards. Shuffle the job cards into a face-down pile.

setup.art: Two players, each with four model cards in their hands, with a pile of jobs between them.
setup.caption: 2. Deal four model cards to each player. Put the other model cards face up in the middle.

setup.art: A player laying one model card on a job card and giving a reason, while another player listens with a challenge card ready.
setup.caption: 3. Turn over a job card, choose a model card and say why. Others may challenge you.

items.f: JOB. You are at a station and want to know where to change trains.
items.b: Best model: The straight-line metro map. It shows the lines and the changes clearly. The distances do not matter for this job.

items.f: JOB. An engineer must dig a tunnel between two stations.
items.b: Best model: The true-path track map. The tunnel must follow the real ground, so true bends and distances matter.

items.f: JOB. A class wants to see the real shapes of Africa and India.
items.b: Best model: A globe. A globe keeps shapes and sizes without stretching.

items.f: JOB. A class wants one sheet that shows every land on the wall.
items.b: Best model: A flat wall map of the world. One flat sheet shows everything at once, though it must stretch some part.

items.f: JOB. You want to remember how your hibiscus looked on Tuesday.
items.b: Best model: A photograph. A photograph keeps one real flower as it was on one day.

items.f: JOB. You want to teach a younger child the parts of any flower.
items.b: Best model: A labelled diagram. A diagram names the parts that every flower of that kind has.

items.f: JOB. A forecaster wants to work out tomorrow's rain.
items.b: Best model: A computer model made of numbers. Only a numbers model can step the weather forward hour by hour.

items.f: JOB. A class wants to show how a Sun, Earth and Moon line up for an eclipse.
items.b: Best model: A small physical model you can hold. A model on wire arms can be turned and looked at from behind.

items.f: JOB. You want to help a friend picture how electricity flows in a wire.
items.b: Best model: An analogy in words. Water in a pipe is easy to picture, though the likeness stops.

items.f: JOB. You want to work out how far a bus goes in 3 hours at 40 kilometres an hour.
items.b: Best model: A rule with numbers. Distance equals speed multiplied by time gives the answer: 120 kilometres.

items.f: JOB. A bird-watcher wants a record of the exact marks on one bird she saw in her garden today.
items.b: Best model: A photograph. A photograph keeps the exact marks of that one bird. A labelled diagram would also work. Either answer can be defended.

items.f: JOB. A scientist wants to show how heat makes water in a pan rise at the middle and sink at the sides.
items.b: Best model: A labelled diagram. Arrows show which way the water moves. A computer model would also work. Either answer can be defended.

items.f: JOB. A shop wants to show how a very large bridge would look before it is built.
items.b: Best model: A small physical model you can hold. A scale model shows the look in three dimensions. A computer model would also work. Either answer can be defended.

items.f: JOB. A teacher wants to explain how fast a wave of a stadium crowd goes.
items.b: Best model: A rule with numbers. Speed is distance over time, and the class can count it. An analogy with water waves would also work. Either answer can be defended.

items.f: JOB. A museum wants a child to feel how big the Earth is, in a handful.
items.b: Best model: A globe. A globe is a model you can hold. A physical model of any kind would also help. Either answer can be defended.

items.f: JOB. A scientist wants to guess where a cyclone will cross the coast in two days.
items.b: Best model: A computer model made of numbers. A weather model steps the air forward in time. A map alone cannot do it.

printables.title: 10 model cards (what it shows and what it leaves out on the back)

items.f: MODEL. The straight-line metro map. Shows each line as a straight stroke, with the stations spaced evenly along it.
items.b: It leaves out true distances and the real bends of the track. It breaks if you use it to guess how far apart two stations are.

items.f: MODEL. The true-path track map. Shows where the tracks really run under the streets.
items.b: It is crowded with every bend and detail, so it is hard to read on a platform. It breaks for a person who only wants to know where to change.

items.f: MODEL. A globe. Shows the shapes, sizes and places of the lands without stretching them.
items.b: It leaves out small detail and it cannot be folded into a pocket. It breaks if you want to see the whole Earth at once.

items.f: MODEL. A flat wall map of the world. Shows every land on one sheet that you can see at once.
items.b: It leaves out true sizes, because it must stretch some part. It breaks if you use it to compare the area of Greenland and Africa.

items.f: MODEL. A photograph. Shows one real thing as it looked at one moment, with every detail the camera caught.
items.b: It leaves out the names of the parts and what is inside. It breaks if you want to understand what every one of that kind has in common.

items.f: MODEL. A labelled diagram. Shows the parts of one kind of thing with plain lines, names and arrows.
items.b: It leaves out the shine, the shadows and the odd details. It breaks if you want to know how this one particular thing looks.

items.f: MODEL. A computer model made of numbers. Shows how a thing may change over time, by working through rules again and again.
items.b: It leaves out everything it has no numbers for. It breaks if its starting numbers are wrong, or if it is used far from what it was built for.

items.f: MODEL. A small physical model you can hold. Shows the shape of a thing in three dimensions, so that you can turn it and look from behind.
items.b: It leaves out the real material and the real size. It breaks if you use it to guess how strong the real thing is.

items.f: MODEL. An analogy in words. Shows what is new by comparing it with what you already know, such as 'the heart is like a pump'.
items.b: It leaves out where the likeness stops. It breaks if you trust it in places where the two things are different.

items.f: MODEL. A rule with numbers. Shows how one quantity depends on another, such as distance equals speed multiplied by time.
items.b: It leaves out the look and the feel of the thing. It breaks if the rule holds only when the speed is steady.

printables.title: Score sheet to copy by hand: one row for each job, with columns for each player's points
items: Job 1 to job 16. Write 2 points for the best model, 1 point for a good argument, 0 for a weak one.

rules: There are 10 model cards. Each model has a plain name, what it shows and, on the back, what it leaves out and where it breaks.
Shuffle the 16 job cards into a face-down pile. Lay all 10 model cards face up in the middle, where everyone can see them.
On your turn, turn over the top job card and read the job aloud, keeping the back hidden. Pick the model card that you think suits the job best. Point to it and say why in one sentence.
Your turn ends with one challenge. Any other player may name one thing your model leaves out that the job needs. If you have an answer, say it. If not, you lose 1 point.

Then turn the job card over and read the best model and the reason. If your model is the best one, you score 2 points. If it is not, but all players agree that your reason is good, you score 1 point. If the card says that two answers can be defended, either one scores 2 points.
The job card goes under the pile of used jobs. The next player turns up a new job.

When the job cards run out, add up the points. The player with the most points wins. If there is a tie, the player who gave the best argument chooses a model card for a last job that the players make up.
When playing alone, turn up all 16 jobs one at a time, choose from all 10 models and score yourself. Try to beat your own score the next day.

flow.do: Cut out the 16 job cards and the 10 model cards. Read all the model cards aloud together. Say what each one shows and what it leaves out. Shuffle the job cards and lay the model cards face up in the middle.
flow.say: Here are ten kinds of model. Each one is good for some jobs and bad for others. Which would you use to find a train change? Which for a tunnel?
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Read the ten models. Lay them face up.
flow.parent: Cutting is for the grown-up if the child is under 8. Keep the cards in an envelope. A game for one child can be played alone, using all ten models.

flow.do: Play the game. Each player turns up a job card, chooses a model card from their hand, says why, takes one challenge and scores. Read the back of each job card aloud, and ask the other player if they agree.
flow.say: Turn up a job. Pick the model you think is best. Tell us why. Then we will see if anyone can find a problem with it.
flow.kid: Take turns. Turn up a job. Pick a model. Say why. Then score.

ask.q: Which job had two models that could both be defended? What would you say for each?
good: The bird-watcher job, because a photograph and a labelled diagram can both be defended.
The bridge job, because a physical model and a computer model both work.
Any job where the reasons for two models were both good.

flow.parent: Let the children argue. The game is meant to show that every model leaves something out and that the best choice depends on the job. Score honestly, but do not let a point matter more than the talk.

flow.do: When the jobs run out, add up the scores. Ask each player which model was used most, and which job was hardest.
flow.say: Add up your points. Which model did you use most? Which job was hardest to match, and why?
flow.kid: Add up your points. Say which job was hardest.

ask.q: Is there a model that is the best for every job? Why or why not?
good: No. Each one leaves something out, and the job decides what can be left out.
A model that kept everything would be as big and as hard to use as the real thing.
Any answer that links the job to the choice.

flow.think: Was there a job for which none of the ten models was good enough? What would you make?
flow.parent: Put the cards back in the envelope for next time. The game can be extended by writing new job cards.

games.title: The waggle dance treasure hunt: read a dance like a bee
games.context: This is a hide-and-find game based on how honeybees tell each other where flowers are. One player is the bee who dances, and the other is her sister who reads the dance and finds the treat.

setup.art: A hall with a window at one end, and a child dancing on a paper circle in the middle of the floor while a parent watches.
setup.caption: 1. Pick a window as the 'Sun'. The dancer stands on a sheet of paper in the middle of the room.

setup.art: A child with a dance card in her hand, while a small treat is placed on the floor behind her, out of sight.
setup.caption: 2. The dancer draws a card, hides a treat as the card says, and returns to the sheet.

setup.art: A parent following the dancer's run towards a hidden treat, counting steps aloud.
setup.caption: 3. The dancer waggles. The sister reads the dance, walks the steps and finds the treat.

items.b: Hide the treat 6 steps straight towards the window.

items.f: Direction: a quarter-turn to the left of the window. Waggle for 2 seconds.
items.b: Hide the treat 6 steps a quarter-turn to the left of the window.

items.f: Direction: a quarter-turn to the left of the window. Waggle for 4 seconds.
items.b: Hide the treat 12 steps a quarter-turn to the left of the window.

items.f: Direction: directly away from the window. Waggle for 3 seconds.
items.b: Hide the treat 9 steps directly away from the window.

items.f: Direction: half of a quarter-turn to the right of the window. Waggle for 3 seconds.

items.f: Direction: half of a quarter-turn to the left of the window. Waggle for 3 seconds.
items.b: Hide the treat 9 steps half of a quarter-turn to the left of the window.
