items.b: Hide the treat 15 steps straight towards the window.

printables.title: How to read the dance, to copy by hand on a small card
items: Everyone faces the window. Right and left mean your own right and left when you face it. Straight towards the window means the treat is that way. A quarter-turn is as far round as the corner of a room. One second of waggle means 3 steps.

rules: One player is the bee. The other is her sister. A window or a lamp stands for the Sun. Put the cards face down in a pile.
The sister waits out of the room, or with her eyes shut. The bee draws a dance card and reads the front without showing it. She hides a small treat on the floor, as the back says.

The sister comes back and watches. The bee stands on a sheet of paper and dances. She walks in a straight line in the direction on the card, waggling her hips for the time on the card. Then she comes back to the paper.

The sister reads the dance. She decides which way to go from the direction and how many steps from the time. One second of waggle is 3 steps. She walks that way from the paper and picks up the treat if she finds it.
The bee shows the back of the card. If the sister found the treat, both score 1 point. If she was off by one step or less, both score 1 point too. Then swap roles.
Play 6 rounds, three each. You are a team and add up your points together. With 5 or more points you win. With fewer, play the six rounds again.
Real bees use the angle to the Sun and about one second for every kilometre, so the game is a scale model of their dance.

flow.do: Choose a room or terrace with a window or a lamp at one end, and at least 15 steps of clear floor. Cut out the dance cards. Put a sheet of paper on the floor to be the dance floor. Explain that a bee tells others where flowers are with a dance.
flow.say: A bee who has found flowers comes home and dances. Her dance says which way and how far. Today we play the dance with a window as the Sun.
flow.kid: Pick a window as the Sun. Put a sheet of paper on the floor.
flow.parent: A bee dances on the comb in the dark hive and 'straight up' stands for the direction of the Sun. The game puts the window where the Sun would be. Do not play on a slippery floor and clear away anything to trip on.

flow.do: Play 6 rounds, three each. In each round the bee reads a card, hides the treat and dances. The sister finds the treat and the pair check the card.
flow.say: Draw a card. Hide the treat. Dance it. Now your sister reads the dance. Where is the treat?
flow.kid: Draw a card. Hide the treat. Dance the route. Your sister reads it.

ask.q: What two things did the dance tell the sister, and how did she use them?
good: Which way to go, and how far, from the time of the waggle.
Direction and distance, which is all that is needed to find a place.
Any answer that names both.

flow.parent: Use a treat such as a raisin or a pebble, and eat or put it away afterwards. A child under 8 can dance and read with a grown-up helping. Make the direction clear with an arm held out. The sister can count the seconds of waggle aloud, one by one, or the bee can wave an arm for each second.

flow.do: Ask what the dance leaves out and what it shows. Ask what a bee's dance cannot tell the other bees.
flow.say: The dance does not tell the colour of the flower or what it smells like. What does it show clearly?
flow.kid: Say what the dance shows and what it leaves out.

ask.q: What does the dance leave out, and who decided that?
good: The colour and smell of the flowers, and the shape of the way. The bee's way of dancing decides what is left out.
Anything but the direction and the distance.
Any answer that names something left out.

flow.think: A bee's dance is a model made by a bee. Who else makes models?
flow.parent: Real bees also carry the smell of the flowers on their bodies. They share nectar too, so the dance is only a part of what the others know.

worksheets.title: What a model is and what it leaves out (core)
worksheets.context: This sheet checks what a model is, the kinds of model, how a diagram differs from a picture, and what every model leaves out.

items.p: A plastic model of a heart is in a school lab. What is it for?
opts: To work as a real heart
To show the parts of a heart clearly
To be a smaller copy with nothing left out
items.why: A model is made to show something clearly, not to do the real thing's job. Choosing the last option treats a model as a perfect copy, but every model leaves something out.

items.p: A good model keeps every detail of the real thing.
items.why: False. A model that kept every detail would be as big and as hard to use as the real thing. Leaving things out is what makes a model clear.

items.p: Sort each one into physical model or diagram.
items: a plastic skeleton in a school lab
a drawing of the digestive system with arrows
a labelled drawing of a leaf
items.a: as given
items.why: A physical model is an object you can hold and turn round. A diagram is a simple drawing with labels, and often arrows, made to explain.

items.p: Match each one to what it does.
pairs: A photograph of one hibiscus
shows that one flower on one day, with its shadow
A diagram of a hibiscus
shows what every flower of that kind has, with names
An arrow in a diagram
shows which way something moves
A label
names a part
items.a: as given
items.why: A photograph keeps whatever the camera caught. A diagram keeps only what its maker chose, and adds labels and arrows that are not in the real flower.

items.p: A globe shows the shapes of the lands but leaves out ____.
items.why: A globe is made to show the shapes and places of the lands. Rain, traffic and smells are left out on purpose, so that the shapes can be seen clearly.

items.p: Put these steps in order for finding out what is inside a sealed box.
a: Draw your first model of the inside
Predict what a new tilt will do
Change the drawing if the test disagrees
items.why: You need clues before you can draw. A prediction comes from the drawing, a test comes from the prediction, and the test decides if the drawing must change.

items.p: Think of your classroom. Name two things you would leave out of a map of it, and say why.
items.a: Any two things, such as the colour of the walls or what is on the notice board, with a reason about what the reader needs. A strong answer says the map is for finding things, so only the things that help are kept.
items.why: A good answer names two things and gives a reason tied to the job of the map.

items.p: Which of these can you pick up and turn round to look at from behind?
opts: A diagram of a flower
A map of India on paper
A model of the Sun, Earth and Moon on wire arms
items.why: A physical model is a solid object. A diagram and a map are drawings on paper, so you can only look at them from the front.

items.p: A diagram of a flower stands for every flower of that kind. It leaves out one flower's shadow.
items.why: True. A diagram keeps what all flowers of that kind share. A photograph keeps the shadow, the ant and everything else that was there at that moment.

items.p: A new child needs a school map. One shows every tree and bench. Another shows only the gate, classrooms and library.

views.who: A child who likes details (an imagined view)
views.says: Draw every tree, bench and window. Then the map is a true picture.

views.who: A child who likes clear maps (an imagined view)
views.says: Draw only the gate, the classrooms and the library, with arrows. Then the map is easy to follow.

items.ask: Which map would help the new child find the library on the first morning? Could the first one also be useful?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer says the second map is quicker to read for finding the library. The first could be useful for a different job, such as finding a tree to sit under. Neither is wrong, and each has a job.
items.why: The first map keeps more but is harder to read. The second keeps less but is clearer for one job. This is the trade-off in every model.

items.p: An orange turns in torchlight and a dot on it goes from light to dark. What does the orange stand for?
opts: The Sun, which moves
The Moon, which glows
The Earth, which turns
items.why: In this model the orange is the Earth and the torch is the Sun. Day and night come from the Earth turning, which carries each place into the light and out of it.

items.p: A map has a box that says a blue line means a river. What is that box for?
opts: To explain what the signs and colours mean
To make the map prettier
To show how big the real place is
items.why: The box is called a key. It tells the reader what each sign and colour stands for. The size of the real place is told by the scale, which is a different part of a map.

items.p: A globe has a scale of 1 centimetre for every 425 kilometres. How many kilometres are 4 centimetres on the globe?
items.why: Each centimetre stands for 425 kilometres, so 4 centimetres stand for 4 × 425 = 1,700 kilometres.

items.p: A marble stops with a click in the middle of a box. It still rolls along the far edge. Draw the inside.
items.a: A rectangle with a wall drawn across the middle, and a gap between the end of the wall and the far side. The marble is shown on one side. A question mark or note says what is not certain, such as the wall's height.
items.why: The marble stopping in the middle says there is a wall. Rolling on only along the far edge says there is a gap there. A good model uses each clue, and a good drawing shows what is still a guess.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? A globe, a plastic skeleton, a sparrow, a diagram of a leaf.
items.a: The sparrow, because a sparrow is a real bird and not a model of one. The other three are models made to stand for something real.
items.why: A model stands for a real thing. A living bird is a real being, and not a model of anything.

items.p: Why can one thing, such as a town, have more than one good model?
items.a: Because different jobs need different things kept. A map for drivers keeps roads, and a map for walkers keeps paths and steps. Each leaves out what the other needs.
items.why: A strong answer names a job for each model and what each leaves out.

worksheets.title: Scale, maps and changing a model (stretch)
worksheets.context: This sheet goes further into scale, why flat maps stretch, how models are tested and changed, and where a comparison stops.

items.p: A diagram of the solar system has the words 'not to scale'. What do they say?
opts: The whole diagram is wrong
The sizes or distances are not true to the real thing
The planets are drawn at their true sizes
items.why: The words warn the reader that something was changed to fit the page. The planets and distances are not in true proportion, but the order of the planets can still be right.

items.p: A 30 centimetre globe stands for the Earth, which is 12,742 kilometres across. So 1 centimetre stands for about ____ kilometres.
items.why: 12,742 ÷ 30 is close to 425. Each centimetre on the globe stands for 425 kilometres of the real Earth, roughly.

items.p: On a flat world map Greenland looks about as big as Africa, so the two lands are about the same size.
items.why: False. Africa is about 14 times larger than Greenland. A flat map must stretch some part of the round Earth, and this map stretches the lands near the top.

items.p: A model predicts that a spot stays lit. A test shows it going dark. What is best?
opts: Say the torch must be broken
Check the test, then change the model if it still disagrees
Ignore the test and keep the model
items.why: A test that disagrees is information. First check that the test was fair, then change the model if it still disagrees. Blaming the torch or ignoring the test keeps the model safe, but teaches nothing.

items.p: Match each comparison to where it stops being like the real thing.
pairs: The heart is like a pump
A pump does not start beating by itself
Electricity in a wire is like water in a pipe
A cut wire does not spill electricity on the floor
A flat map is like the land
A flat map stretches some lands, because the Earth is round
items.a: as given
items.why: Every analogy is right in some ways and wrong in others. The useful question is where the likeness stops.

items.p: Put these models of the atom in the order they were made, oldest first.
a: Thomson: a soft ball with small bits dotted through it (1904)
Rutherford: a tiny hard centre with most of the space empty (1911)
items.why: Each model changed when new evidence came. Particles that bounced straight back from gold in 1909 could not happen with a soft ball, so Rutherford drew a new model.

items.p: Your model says a marble cannot pass the middle. You see it pass. Give two things you could do.
items.a: Check the tilt was done as planned and try again. Change the drawing, for example by adding a gap. Predict a new tilt from the changed drawing and test that.
items.why: A strong answer treats the surprise as a clue and changes the model, then tests the new model with a new prediction.

items.p: A plan of a school is made to help a new child find the library. Sort each thing.
items: the way from the gate, with arrows
items.a: as given
items.why: The plan is made for finding the way. It keeps the places and the route, and leaves out what does not help with that job.

items.p: Is a model that gives right answers also true?

views.who: A scientist who thinks it is (an imagined view)
views.says: The atom model worked, and the atom was later photographed. Models that work are probably the way the world really is.

views.who: A scientist who thinks it is only a tool (an imagined view)
views.says: Ptolemy's model of the sky worked for about 1,400 years and was wrong. A model that works may only be a handy tool.

items.ask: Which view do you find stronger, or do you need more evidence? What would help you decide?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer uses both examples and notes that nobody has a sure way to tell in advance which kind a model is. Scientists still argue about it.
items.why: The atom began as a model and was later seen as a real thing. Ptolemy's model gave right answers and was not built like the sky. Both histories are true.

items.p: Why does a diagram have labels and arrows that the real thing does not have?
opts: The real thing is always missing them
They are added to explain, not to copy
They make the diagram prettier
items.why: A diagram is made to be understood. Labels name the parts and arrows show what moves. A copy of the real thing would have neither.

items.p: If a model gives right answers, it must be built in the same way as the real thing.
items.why: False. Ptolemy's model of circles on circles gave right answers for about 1,400 years, though the Earth is not at the centre. Right answers do not show that the inside is right.

items.p: Which clue best shows that a wall across the middle of a sealed box is there?
opts: A marble rolls to a corner and stays
A marble stops at the middle every time
The box feels heavy
items.why: A marble that always stops at the same line in the middle says there is something there. Rolling to a corner and staying is what you would get with no wall.

items.p: Draw water going from a tap into a glass, with labels and arrows. Then write one thing you left out.
items.a: A tap, a glass and an arrow showing water moving down, with labels such as 'tap', 'water' and 'glass'. A good answer names a left-out thing, such as the pipe in the wall, the splashes or the colour of the glass.
items.why: A diagram has plain lines, labels and arrows. Everything not needed to explain the flow is left out.

items.p: A model is 50 times smaller than a bridge 300 metres long. How long is the model, in metres?
items.why: 300 ÷ 50 = 6. The model is 6 metres long. Every length on it is 50 times smaller than the real one.

items.p: Which one is a model made of words?
opts: A globe
'The heart is like a pump'
A plastic skeleton
items.why: A comparison in words is called an analogy. A globe and a plastic skeleton are physical models, which are objects you can hold.

items.p: What must a diagram of the solar system change to fit on a page? How can the maker be honest about it?
items.a: The distances are squeezed and the planets drawn too big. The maker can write 'not to scale' on the diagram.
items.why: A strong answer names the change and the honest note.

worksheets.title: Right answers, wrong insides and open questions (challenge)
worksheets.context: This sheet looks at faulty reasoning about models, and at questions about models that scientists still argue about.

items.p: Ptolemy's model of the sky predicted the planets well for about 1,400 years. What does that show?
opts: It was built just as the sky is built
A model can predict well and still be wrong inside
Predictions never matter
items.why: The model used circles on circles, which can copy almost any path. It gave right answers and was still wrong about the Earth being at the centre.

items.p: A map that kept every detail of a city would be the best map.
items.why: False. It would be as large as the city and as hard to use. A map is useful because the maker chose what to leave out.

items.p: Why does Greenland look so big on a flat map of the world?
opts: The map must stretch some part of a round Earth
Greenland is as big as Africa
The mapmaker made a careless mistake
items.why: A round surface cannot be flattened without stretching or tearing, like an orange peel. The usual map stretches the lands near the top.

items.p: A friend says, 'My model must be right, because it has never been wrong.' What test could still show it wrong?
items.a: A new prediction in a new situation that the model has never been tried on, one that could fail. Only a test that could go wrong can show that a model is right so far.
items.why: A model that has only been used where it is known to work has not been tested hard.

items.p: Put these in the order they happened in the story of the tongue map.
a: A German study of 1901 finds tiny differences in taste across the tongue
A 1942 book draws the tiny differences as firm zones
The zone map is copied from book to book
A 1974 test shows that every part of the tongue can sense every taste
items.why: A small, careful result was redrawn as a neat map with firm borders. The neat map was copied without being tested, until someone tested it again.

items.p: Match each model to what it cannot tell you.
pairs: A flat world map
the true sizes of lands near the top
A weather forecast model
what the weather will be, for certain, on your street
A plastic skeleton
how strong a real bone is
A diagram of a flower
the colour of your own hibiscus
items.a: as given
items.why: Every model leaves something out. Asking what it leaves out tells you what not to use it for.

items.p: On a globe, 1 centimetre is 425 kilometres. Everest is 9 kilometres high. On the globe it is ____ millimetres.
items.why: 9 ÷ 425 is about 0.02 centimetres, which is 0.2 of a millimetre. That is too small to feel on a globe.

items.p: A model that is very useful for one job is useful for every job.
items.why: False. A metro map is perfect for choosing where to change, and no use for digging a tunnel. Each model suits the job it was made for.

items.p: Is the picture in your mind of a friend a model?

views.who: A philosopher who says yes (an imagined view)
views.says: Your idea of a friend keeps a few features, such as the voice and the face, and leaves out most of her life. That is what a model does.

views.who: A philosopher who says no (an imagined view)
views.says: A model is made on purpose to explain. Knowing a friend is not a drawing or a rule. It is knowing a living person.

items.ask: Which view do you find more convincing? What would the picture in your mind leave out?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer notices that the picture in the mind does leave out most of the friend, and asks whether being made on purpose matters. This question has no single answer.
items.why: Both views can be defended. The first sees the likeness to a model. The second sees that knowing a person is more than a drawing.

items.p: Nobody can open an atom. How can scientists still test a model of it?
opts: They cannot, so every model of the atom is only a guess
They predict what will happen when something hits it, then look
They open it with a very small tool
items.why: A model of the atom predicts what will happen, for example when fast particles hit gold. Then people look. The bounces that a soft ball could not give led to a new model.

items.p: The eye has a blind spot, yet we see no hole. Give one reason for calling seeing a model, and one against.
items.a: For: the brain fills the gap with a guess made from what lies around it, so part of what we see is supplied. Against: the eye still receives real light from the world, and what we see changes when the world changes.
items.why: A strong answer gives a reason on each side and does not claim the question is settled.

items.p: Which one is NOT a physical model?
opts: A plastic heart in a lab
A doll's house
The rule: distance equals speed times time
items.why: A physical model is an object you can hold. The rule is a model made of numbers and words, and it has no shape to hold.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? A labelled diagram, a metro map, a photograph, a globe.
items.a: The photograph, because it keeps whatever the camera happened to catch. The other three are made by choosing what to keep.
items.why: A photograph records a moment. The others are made on purpose, with parts kept and parts left out.

items.p: Draw two models of a mango: one for choosing a ripe mango, one for planting its seed. Say what each leaves out.
items.a: One shows the outside, with the colour, the skin and the smell. The other shows the inside, with the flesh and the flat seed. Each leaves out what the other needs.
items.why: The first model is for a buyer, so the outside matters. The second is for a grower, so the seed matters. The job decides what to keep.

items.p: A diagram of a sparrow is 30 centimetres long. The real bird is 15 centimetres. How many times bigger is the diagram?
items.why: 30 ÷ 15 = 2. The diagram is twice the size of the real bird. Scale tells you how a model compares with the real thing.

items.p: Scientists still argue about whether a model that works is true. Write one test that might help, and say why.
items.a: Any test with a reason. One test is to use the model to predict something new and then check it. Another is to look with a new instrument at what the model says is there.
items.why: A strong answer picks a test that could show the model wrong.

quiz.p: A friend says a model must be exactly like the real thing. What is the best reply?
opts: A model keeps what matters for a job and leaves out the rest
Yes, otherwise it is only a drawing
Only scientists may call something a model
quiz.why: A model is a tool for understanding. Making an exact copy would give you the whole world again, and no clearer picture of it.

quiz.p: A lab has a plastic eye that comes apart and a labelled chart of the eye. Which is the physical model?
opts: The labelled chart
Both of them
The plastic eye
quiz.why: A physical model is an object you can hold and turn round. A labelled chart is a diagram, which is a model on paper.

quiz.p: A diagram of a hibiscus helps you with a hibiscus you have never seen. Why?
opts: It is a photograph of the same flower
It shows what all flowers of that kind have
It shows the exact shadow
quiz.why: A diagram stands for every flower of that kind, with parts named. A photograph shows only one flower as it looked once.

quiz.p: A diagram of a heart is not red. Is that a fault?
opts: Yes, the heart is red
No, colour is not needed for its job
Yes, every diagram must have colour
quiz.why: A diagram keeps what its job needs, here the parts and the way blood flows. A model is not faulty because it leaves something out.

quiz.p: A mapmaker flattens a round globe onto paper. What cannot be avoided?
opts: Some sizes or shapes are stretched
Everything stays true in size and shape
Nothing changes near the top
quiz.why: A round surface cannot be flattened without stretching or tearing, as an orange peel shows. Each flat map chooses which wrongness to accept.

quiz.p: A leaning ball in torchlight predicts a season with no sunset near the poles. Why is a prediction like that valuable?
opts: It proves the model right in every way
We can check it against the real world
It is a guess that nobody can check
quiz.why: A prediction that can be checked tests the model. If it comes true, the model is trusted a little more. It does not prove the model is built just as the world is.

quiz.p: A model gives right answers for 100 years. Is it certain to be built like the real thing?
opts: Yes, that proves it
No, a wrong model can still predict well
Yes, if scientists agree
quiz.why: Ptolemy's model of the sky worked for about 1,400 years and the Earth is not at the centre. Right answers show a model is useful, not that it is built like the world.

quiz.p: You cannot open a sealed box. What is the best way to improve your drawing of what is inside?
opts: Predict a new tilt, test it and change the drawing if wrong
Guess harder
Shake it as hard as you can
quiz.why: A prediction that could fail tests the drawing. Shaking hard gives noise, and guessing harder gives no new clues.

quiz.p: Gold foil bounced a few fast particles straight back. What does this show about models?
opts: Models are always wrong
Models change when new evidence disagrees
A first model should never be changed
quiz.why: The soft-ball model of the atom could not give bounces like this. So Rutherford made a new model. A model is improved by evidence that disagrees with it.

quiz.p: One metro map has straight strokes and another shows the true track. Which one is wrong?
opts: The straight one, because it bends the tracks
Neither, because each suits a different job
The true one, because it is hard to read
quiz.why: The straight one is right for finding where to change. The true one is right for an engineer who digs. Neither is the real metro.

quiz.p: Why do engineers test a small model of a dam before building the real one?
opts: A model is always stronger than the real dam
A mistake in a model costs far less
A model needs no tests
quiz.why: A model can be wrecked and rebuilt cheaply. A mistake in a real dam could cost lives. The model leaves out some things, so engineers also test in other ways.

quiz.p: One friend will swim in a river. Another will build a dam on it. Why might they need different models?
opts: Each job needs different things kept in the model
Models of rivers are all the same
Only one of them needs a model
quiz.why: The swimmer needs where the water is deep and where it flows fast. The builder needs the ground, the width and how much water comes. Each model keeps what its job needs.

quiz.p: Which of these has labels and arrows that are not in the real thing?
opts: A photograph
A diagram
A mirror
quiz.why: A diagram adds labels and arrows to explain. A photograph and a mirror show what is there, without choosing or adding.

quiz.p: Which question do scientists still argue about?
opts: Does a globe have a scale?
Does a model that works always show how the world is built?
Can a diagram have arrows?
quiz.why: The first and third are settled by looking. Whether a good model is true or only useful is an old argument. Ptolemy's model and the atom model each show a side of it.

maths.problem: A classroom globe is 30 centimetres across. The real Earth is 12,742 kilometres across. How many kilometres does 1 centimetre of the globe stand for?
maths.explain: 12,742 ÷ 30 comes to 424.7. Round it to 425. So 1 centimetre of the globe is 425 kilometres of the Earth.
maths.context: This problem finds the scale of a globe from two sizes.
maths.why_maths: A scale is a ratio between the model and the real thing. Once you know it, every length on the model can be turned into a real length.

maths.problem: In a model of the solar system the Sun is 22 centimetres across. The real Sun is about 1.4 million kilometres across, and the Earth is 150 million kilometres from it. About how far from the Sun does the Earth go in the model?
maths.explain: The Sun is 22 centimetres in the model, so 1 centimetre is about 64,000 kilometres. 150,000,000 ÷ 64,000 is about 2,340. So the Earth is about 2,340 centimetres away, which is about 23 metres.
maths.context: This problem uses the Sun's size to find the scale, then uses the scale to place the Earth.
maths.why_maths: The same scale must be used for sizes and distances, or the model is not true. This is the maths behind the 32 steps in the walk.

maths.problem: A model of a 120-metre bridge is 60 centimetres long. How many centimetres of the real bridge does 1 centimetre of the model stand for? A tower on the real bridge is 40 metres tall. How tall is the tower on the model?
maths.answer: 200 centimetres, which is 2 metres. The model tower is 20 centimetres tall.
maths.explain: 120 metres is 12,000 centimetres. 12,000 ÷ 60 is 200. So 1 centimetre stands for 200 centimetres. The tower is 4,000 centimetres, and 4,000 ÷ 200 is 20 centimetres.
maths.context: This problem finds a scale from one length and uses it for another.
maths.why_maths: A scale model keeps every length in the same ratio. One known pair of lengths gives all the rest.

maths.problem: Greenland covers about 2.2 million square kilometres, and Africa about 30.4 million. On a common classroom map they look about the same size. About how many times is Greenland stretched, compared with Africa?
maths.explain: 30.4 ÷ 2.2 is about 13.8, so about 14. Africa is 14 times larger, yet it is drawn the same size as Greenland. So Greenland has been stretched by about 14 times in area, compared with Africa.
maths.context: This problem compares two areas on a flat map with their real areas.
maths.why_maths: A map that stretches the lands near the top changes areas by a ratio. Comparing the real ratio with the drawn ratio shows how big the stretch is.

maths.problem: A honeybee waggles for 3 seconds, and the dance means about one second for each kilometre. A bee flies about 7 metres each second. About how long will her sisters take to fly to the flowers?
maths.explain: 3 seconds of waggle means about 3 kilometres, which is 3,000 metres. 3,000 ÷ 7 is about 430 seconds. 430 ÷ 60 is about 7 minutes.
maths.context: This problem reads a bee's dance as a model of a journey, then finds the time of the journey.
maths.why_maths: The dance turns a distance into a time, and speed turns the distance back into a time of flight. Two ratios are chained.

maths.problem: A dot vanishes into the blind spot when it is 10 centimetres from the cross and your eye is 35 centimetres away. How far apart must the cross and dot be for the dot to vanish when your eye is 70 centimetres away?
maths.explain: The blind spot sits at a fixed angle from where you look. If you move twice as far away, the gap on the paper must be twice as wide. 10 × 2 = 20.
maths.context: This problem uses the blind-spot test to see how a fixed angle works at different distances.
maths.why_maths: A fixed angle gives a gap that grows in proportion with the distance. This is why the dot vanishes at a different place when you move the paper.

spotted.text: At a metro station in Chennai, Kochi, Delhi or Kolkata, look at the line map on the wall or the door. Notice that the stations are evenly spaced and the lines are straight. The real tracks bend, and the real stations are not evenly apart.
spotted.art: A metro map above a train door with straight coloured lines and evenly spaced dots.

spotted.text: Open a map on a phone and zoom in and out. Notice that some things appear when you zoom in, such as small lanes and shop names, and others vanish when you zoom out. Each zoom has left out what it does not need.
spotted.art: A phone screen showing a map zoomed out with only big roads, and the same place zoomed in with small lanes.

spotted.text: Find a floor plan in a flat advertisement or in the builder's brochure. Notice what it shows, such as walls, doors and room sizes. Notice what it leaves out, such as the view and the noise from the road.
spotted.art: A builder's brochure open to a simple floor plan with room labels.

spotted.text: Look at the heart or the digestive system in your science textbook. Notice the labels and arrows. Then look at a photograph of a real heart, if you can find one, and notice how different they look.
spotted.art: A textbook diagram of the heart with labels, beside a small photo of a real heart.

spotted.text: When the weather forecast on TV or a phone says 'rain tomorrow, 70 per cent', notice that this is a prediction from a model. It is not a certain fact. Check the next day and see if it was right.
spotted.art: A phone weather app showing a cloud and the number 70 per cent.

spotted.text: On a cricket broadcast, look at the diagram of where each run was scored, or the line showing a ball's path. It is a model of the match, with the grass and the crowd taken away.
spotted.art: A television showing a cricket ground drawn as an oval with coloured lines from the middle.

spotted.text: Look at a bus route board or a train route chart in your town. Notice that it shows the stops in order and nothing else, like a model made for one job.
spotted.art: A bus shelter board with a route drawn as a row of stops joined by a line.

applications: Engineers test small models of bridges and tall buildings in wind tunnels before the real ones are built. A model is placed in a tunnel with a fan, and sensors measure the push of the air. Mistakes are found cheaply.

Forecasters in India use computer models of the air to forecast the monsoon and cyclones. The model is stepped forward in time, and they compare its answer with what they see. In 2013 a forecast of where Cyclone Phailin would cross the coast of Odisha helped move about ten lakh people to safety.
Doctors use plastic models of bones and organs to explain an operation to a patient, and surgeons practise on models before they operate on a person.

Town planners make a map of where a new road should go, then check the map against the land. They use maps of different scales for different jobs, such as one for the whole district and one for a single street.
A tailor makes a paper pattern before cutting the cloth. The pattern is a model of the shirt, and a mistake on paper costs much less than a mistake in cloth.
Teachers and children use diagrams in every science book. Every diagram in a textbook is a model, and a reader can ask what it keeps and what it leaves out.
ask_kids: Think of a map you have used. What did it show, and what did it leave out? Was that a good choice?
If you had to explain your home to someone in a different country, what would you put in a model, and what would you leave out?
Which is better for remembering a friend's face, a photograph or a drawing? Which is better for explaining what a face is made of?
Is the world you see with your eyes a picture, or a model your brain makes? What makes you think so?

warmup.q: What is a map of your school for?
warmup.a: To help a person find places, such as the gate and the classrooms.

warmup.q: What is the difference between a photograph and a drawing?
warmup.a: A photograph records the light that reached a camera. A drawing is made by a person, who chooses what to put in.

warmup.q: Why is a map drawn smaller than the real place?
warmup.a: So that it fits on paper and can be carried. The real place is too big to hold.

warmup.q: What do the words on a drawing of a flower, such as 'petal', do?
warmup.a: They name the parts, so that a reader knows what each part is.

warmup.q: Name one thing you can see in your room that is a model of something real.
warmup.a: A toy car, a globe, a doll or a drawing are all models. Any honest answer is fine.

warmup.q: A friend says her picture of a mango looks 'wrong' because it has no stripes. What could you ask?
warmup.a: What the picture is for. A picture for showing a mango's shape does not need stripes.

quiz: A model shows the important features of a thing and leaves other things out.
A model is a tool for clear understanding, and what it leaves out depends on its job.
A diagram is the same thing as a photograph.
A photograph keeps whatever the camera caught. A diagram keeps what its maker chose and adds labels and arrows.
A globe is a physical model of the Earth.
A globe is an object you can hold and turn, with the lands drawn on it.
A flat map of the whole Earth can be right in every way.
A round surface cannot be flattened without stretching or tearing, so every flat map stretches something.
One thing can have more than one good model.
Different jobs need different things kept, so a metro can have a track map and a line map.
A model that gives right answers must be built just like the real thing.
A model can give right answers and still be built differently from the real thing.
Words on a diagram that say 'not to scale' tell you the sizes are not true.
They warn the reader that something was changed to fit the page.
A model that fails a test should be left unchanged.
A test that disagrees tells you something. The model is checked and changed.
